subject_definitions:

<Subject 1> is the person whose appearance comes from <Picture 1> and whose physical motion comes from <Video 1>. Preserve the person's identity, facial features, hairstyle, body proportions, clothing, and overall visual appearance from <Picture 1>.

<Picture 1> is the first frame of [Shot 1], serving as the concrete opening-frame and composition reference for the target video.

<Video 1> is the motion reference for <Subject 1>. It provides the subject's physical movement sequence, gestures, posture changes, body orientation, movement rhythm, timing, and final pose. The target video's background, environment, composition, and visual appearance do not come from <Video 1>.


summary:

[reference generation + keyframe completion] The target video begins exactly from <Picture 1> as the first frame and shows <Subject 1> performing the physical movement sequence demonstrated in <Video 1>.

<Picture 1> is the concrete first-frame reference for [Shot 1] and defines the target video's opening composition, environment, camera viewpoint, subject position, appearance, and initial pose.

<Video 1> is used only as a motion reference for <Subject 1>. Transfer the subject's physical movement sequence, gestures, posture changes, body orientation, rhythm, timing, and final pose from <Video 1> onto <Subject 1>.

Do not use the background, environment, camera composition, lighting setup, or other scene content from <Video 1> as the target video's visual source.


retention_analysis:

<Subject 1> (appears in [Shot 1]): fully_preserved - the person's identity, facial features, hairstyle, body proportions, clothing, and overall visual appearance from <Picture 1> are retained throughout the target video.

<Picture 1> ([Shot 1] first frame): fully_preserved - the image is used as the concrete first frame of the target video, preserving its opening composition, environment, camera viewpoint, subject position, appearance, and initial pose.

<Video 1>: attribute_transfer - only the physical motion performance of the person in <Video 1> is transferred to <Subject 1>, including movement sequence, gestures, posture changes, body orientation, rhythm, timing, and final pose. The visual identity, background, environment, camera composition, lighting, and other scene characteristics of <Video 1> are not transferred.


detailed_description:

The target video is a realistic motion-reference generation with the opening frame anchored to <Picture 1>. The target scene and visual environment are established by <Picture 1>, while the physical performance of <Subject 1> follows the motion demonstrated in <Video 1>.

[Shot 1]

The shot begins directly from <Picture 1>.

At 0.00 seconds into the target video, <Picture 1> is fully referenced as the first frame of [Shot 1]. The first frame must reproduce the composition, environment, camera viewpoint, subject position, subject appearance, clothing, lighting, and initial pose shown in <Picture 1>.

<Subject 1> starts from the exact initial pose and position shown in <Picture 1>.

From this starting state, <Subject 1> begins the physical movement sequence demonstrated in <Video 1>.

Transfer the motion performance from <Video 1> onto <Subject 1> as faithfully as possible. Preserve the movement order, body orientation, arm and hand gestures, leg movements, posture transitions, movement rhythm, timing, acceleration and deceleration, and final pose demonstrated by the reference performance.

The person in <Video 1> is used only as a motion-performance reference. Do not reproduce that person's identity or appearance.

The target video remains in the visual environment established by <Picture 1>. Do not replace or extend the opening environment with the background, location, camera composition, lighting setup, or other visual content from <Video 1>.

<Subject 1> retains the identity and appearance defined by <Picture 1> throughout the entire movement sequence.

Maintain continuous visual and spatial continuity from the first frame of <Picture 1> as the subject transitions naturally into the referenced motion.

End with <Subject 1> in the corresponding final pose from <Video 1>.
